title: Shvetaketu Comes Home
hookLine: a son comes home after twelve years of study, sure he knows it all, and his father asks one question he can't answer
carry: after the doing comes the wish to know brahman
tomorrow: Bhrigu asks his father what Brahman is. why won't his father just say?

cards: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Veda. At twenty-four he comes back.
He's learned all of it, the hymns, the rites, and he walks in, as the text puts it, full of himself, sure he's learned. His father, Uddalaka, lets him settle. Then he asks one question.
Did you ask your teachers for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means.

teach.h: KNOW THE CLAY, KNOW EVERY POT.
teach.b: So Uddalaka shows him. Know one lump of clay, and you know everything made of clay. The pot and the bowl are just names, shapes, words.
What's real is the clay. Shvetaketu is stunned. My teachers can't have known this, he says, or they'd have told me.

And the father begins the teaching we'll hear more of this week: underneath everything there is one reality, which the Upanishads call Brahman. That's Vedanta, the Veda's end, the teaching of the Upanishads.
Its root text, the Brahma Sutra, opens with one short line: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. The great commentators stop on its first word.

Now, after what? Shankara says: after a person learns to tell the lasting from the passing, cools toward rewards, gathers calm, and longs to be free. Ramanuja says: after the study of ritual, the earlier inquiry.
Two readings, kept side by side. Either way, the teaching is plain.
In Hinduism, doing the rites well is not the end of the road. A day comes when a person who has kept the fasts and lit the lamps asks what all of it rests on. That wish is honored, not suspected.
It's where Vedanta begins. Shvetaketu didn't lose his twelve years. He finally asked what they were for.

how: Students of Vedanta traditionally begin the Brahma Sutra with its first line, the wish to know Brahman, read through their lineage's commentary, often Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, and the Chandogya's story of Shvetaketu is one of the best-known ways the Upanishads are taught.

o: a school that says the rites should be stopped
the teaching of the Upanishads: one reality under everything
a set of rules for which rites to do, and when

games.q: Shvetaketu comes home — tap the pairs.
p: studies twelve years, comes home proud
asks for the teaching that makes all known
know it, and every pot is known
now, the wish to know Brahman

s: Uddalaka tells his son the years of study were wasted
he asks what they rest on: the one reality, Brahman, known like clay under every pot.
Shankara and Ramanuja read the Sutra's first word, now, the same way
Shankara puts the readiness in the person; Ramanuja says it comes after the study of ritual.
in Vedanta, wanting to know what everything rests on is where the path begins
the Brahma Sutra opens with that wish, not with a claim.

games.q: you've kept every puja step for years, and one day you wonder what it all rests on. by Vedanta's first line, what is that wondering?
o: a sign your faith is slipping
the wish to know Brahman, where Vedanta begins
a reason to stop doing the rites
games.why: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. like Shvetaketu, the question comes after the doing, and it's honored.

practice: Pick one thing you do out of habit or faith, a prayer, a fast, a lamp, a way you greet your elders, and do it in your mind, step by step. Then let one quiet question rise: what does this rest on? Don't answer it.
Hold the wish to know, the way Shvetaketu finally did. If you pray, you can ask it in the presence of the One you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Vedanta. The Veda's end, the teaching of the Upanishads, which opens with the wish to know Brahman, the one reality under everything. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the school, read as the Veda's end, pointing to the Upanishads.

carryVoice: Your line: after the doing comes the wish to know Brahman. Like Shvetaketu, ask what it all rests on. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1 (Shvetaketu leaves at twelve, returns at twenty-four proud; the teaching by which the unheard is heard; the clay, its names and its reality; 'my teachers cannot have known this')
Brahma Sutra 1.1.1 (now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman)
Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.1 (what the 'now' follows: discernment, dispassion, calm and the rest, longing for freedom)
Ramanuja, Shri Bhashya 1.1.1 (the 'now' follows the knowledge of ritual works)
